newsitem.title: SOUTH AFRICA: Mandela takes whie S African press bosses to task.
newsitem.headline: Mandela takes whie S African press bosses to task.

text.p: President Nelson Mandela told white media bosses on Tuesday their era of supremacy was over but assured them South African press freedom would always be safe.
"The time for white supremacy, for you to dictate to us, is over. It will never come back," Mandela said at a dinner for foreign correspondents in South Africa.

But Mandela, in a combative tone, also attacked black journalists who have accused him of trying to appease whites and not moving fast enough to meet the expectations of the impoverished black masses.

Mandela said he felt betrayed by some black journalists who he said had constantly attacked his policy of reconciliation: "I have told them that as long as they impugn the integrity of my organisation I will hammer them."
He said he had called in black journalists to explain his policy, telling them "reconciliation is the most powerful weapon that we have".
He said his policy had avoided a "Bosnia" in South Africa prior to the 1994 all-race elections that ended apartheid. Yet in the days after that briefing the attacks continued, Mandela said.

Stressing that both he and his ruling African National Congress were committed to a free press, Mandela said: "The media should not be a lapdog, it should be a watchdog to make sure that our famous revolutionaries remain on course."
He said freedom of expression was not only protected by the new constitution and bill of rights but was prized by the ANC.
"Media freedom is not, has not been, and will never be under threat in our country," Mandela said.

"It is in the selfish interest of the ANC that we should have a probing, robust and critical media...a questioning media that seeks to expose the weaknesses of our inherited bureaucracy, security forces, judiciary and indeed the new politicians themselves who can easily be corrupted by power."

But, returning to a point he has made more than once recently, he said "in terms of distribution of wealth and power, ownership, management and senior positions in the media are predominantly in white hands."
"Debate on all these issues will continue for many years... as the Fourth Estate transforms itself to become part of the new South Africa in both word and deed," Mandela added.
Mandela has crossed swords with the media recently, alleging that some senior black newspaper journalists were doing the "dirty work" of their reactionary white bosses by running down his government.
Some editorial writers have warned Mandela that his attacks risk spreading a perception abroad that he would like a tame press.
